The jet fuel alone required for that leg often sits far lower than the price paid at the gate. That spread points to layers of process and constraint that sit on top of the basic physics of flight.
Airlines schedule flights around scarce airport slots that are allocated through long-standing
rules and negotiations. Those slots limit how many planes can depart in a given hour,
so carriers protect the ones they hold by filling them even when marginal revenue is thin.
Distribution systems add another layer. Global distribution services and online travel agencies
take fees that can reach double-digit percentages of the fare. Yield management algorithms
than adjust prices in real-time to protect high-value seats.

Crew costs are fixed once the flight is scheduled,

Airport charges for landing, parking, and terminal use are set by contracts that change slowly
and often include minimum guarantees.
Maintenance reserves and insurance are calculated on fleet-wide averages
rather than per flight marginal wear.
